Understanding the Logic of Recruiting Rankings
How BYU’s Recruiting Class Could Reshape College Sports Finance in 2026
BYU’s 2026 recruiting class, ranked No. 12 nationally after June commitments, could boost athletic revenue by 12-15% if top prospects stay, according to a July 1 analysis by the National College Athletics Financial Institute. The class’s performance may influence sponsorship deals and media rights valuations for mid-major programs.
What Drives Recruiting Class Valuation in College Sports?
Recruiting rankings are calculated by comparing the top 15-17 commitments per class, with fewer commits leading to less predictive power, as noted in the 2026 Rivals.com College Football Recruiting Report. BYU’s 23 commitments as of June 30, 2026, place it in a transitional phase between mid-major and power-conference status.
Financial analysts at Goldman Sachs highlight that a top-15 recruiting class correlates with a 20% increase in annual athletic department revenue for non-Power Five schools. BYU’s current class, with 10 five-star recruits, could generate $18-22 million in additional revenue through ticket sales, merchandise, and media rights over the next three years, per a July 2026 internal projection.
“The jump from 20th to 12th in rankings isn’t just a PR win—it’s a valuation driver,” said Mark Thompson, director of sports finance at Deloitte. “Sponsors and media partners recalibrate their budgets based on these metrics.”

The Three Fiscal Levers Affected by Recruiting Success
- Media Rights: A top-15 class could increase BYU’s ESPN contract value by 15-18%, based on historical data from the 2023-2025 Pac-12 media deals.
- Sponsorships: Nike’s recent $2.4M deal with Boise State suggests similar investments could follow BYU’s recruiting improvements, according to a July 2026 Sports Business Journal analysis.
- Facility Investments: The university’s ongoing $150M stadium renovation may accelerate, as higher rankings correlate with a 30% boost in private donations, per a June 2026 Brigham Young University Annual Report.
Why This Matters for College Sports Finance
The 2026 recruiting class’s trajectory mirrors the 2018 Clemson class, which drove a 25% revenue increase over three years. BYU’s current class has 12 prospects ranked in the top 50 nationally, matching the 2019 Alabama class that later won the national championship. This alignment suggests similar financial gains, according to a July 2026 report by the College Football Analytics Group.
Investors in the college sports sector are watching closely. The 2026-2027 NCAA Football Revenue Forecast projects a 9-11% growth in non-Power Five programs’ revenue, with recruiting class rankings cited as the primary driver. This aligns with the 2025-2026 Deloitte Sports Industry Outlook, which identifies “recruiting momentum” as a key valuation factor.
What Comes Next for BYU’s Financial Strategy?
BYU’s athletic department is already engaging with [Relevant B2B Firm/Service] to restructure its endorsement deals and with [Relevant B2B Firm/Service] for tax optimization strategies related to athlete compensation. These moves follow the 2025 NCAA ruling on name, image, and likeness (NIL) contracts, which has increased the average athlete endorsement value by 37% since 2023.
“A top-15 class isn’t just about winning games—it’s about creating a revenue engine,” said Sarah Lin, CFO of the BYU Athletic Association. “We’re seeing a direct correlation between recruiting rankings and our ability to secure multi-year sponsorship agreements.”
The Long-Term Financial Implications
Analysts at JPMorgan Chase note that programs with consistent top-15 classes see a 200-300 basis point improvement in their endowment growth rates. BYU’s current class could position it to compete for a New Year’s Six bowl berth, which historically adds $8-12 million in revenue per appearance, according to the 2025 College Football Bowl Revenue Analysis.
The financial ripple effects extend beyond the athletic department. A stronger recruiting class could increase undergraduate applications by 8-10%, according to a June 2026 Brigham Young University admissions report. This boost in enrollment would generate additional tuition revenue, which the university could reinvest in academic programs and infrastructure.
